correctness.rationale: Reversal sends the path maximum to \(S-m\) while preserving \(S\), so reversal invariance gives \(\mathbb E[Mg(S)]=\mathbb E[(S-m)g(S)]\). Global sign change sends \((M,S)\) to \((-m,-S)\), and oddness of \(g\) gives \(\mathbb E[Mg(S)]=\mathbb E[mg(S)]\). Combining yields the exact half identity. The covariance, drawdown and range formulas follow algebraically. For iid symmetric increments, \(\operatorname{Var}(S)=n\sigma^2\); Donsker plus maximal-moment uniform integrability gives \(\operatorname{Var}(M)/(n\sigma^2)\to1-2/\pi\), hence the displayed correlation. The inspected checker verifies the exact identities on deliberately nonexchangeable reversal/sign-orbit mixtures and on iid finite walks, while the proof itself is the two-symmetry argument.

value.rationale: The result isolates an exact component of classical maximum theory that survives under very weak dependence: only reversal and global sign symmetry are needed, not independence or exchangeability. The odd-transform family, drawdown/range companions, and explicit nonexchangeable examples make the identity a reusable structural symmetry principle rather than a single iid covariance calculation.

final_claim: If a square-integrable finite increment vector is invariant under reversal and global sign change, then for every integrable odd transform \(g\), \(\mathbb E[M g(S)]=\tfrac12\mathbb E[Sg(S)]\); consequently \(\operatorname{Cov}(M,S)=\tfrac12\operatorname{Var}(S)\), the drawdown and range identities in RESULT.md hold, and under iid symmetric increments with a \(2+\delta\) moment the maximum-endpoint correlation converges to \(1/(2\sqrt{1-2/\pi})\).
limitations: The exact finite-horizon identities require both reversal invariance and global sign symmetry.
The asymptotic correlation additionally assumes iid symmetric increments and a \(2+\delta\) moment.
The iid half-variance specialization lies inside classical random-walk maximum theory; originality is the weaker symmetry class and odd-transform identity.
